summary: Describes how to send Hebrew in electronic mail, using MIME and the ISO-8859-8 character set.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how to send Hebrew text in email using MIME. It specifies ISO-8859-8, a transfer encoding, and headers that tell the recipient how to interpret the message.

questions: how to send hebrew text in email
how should hebrew text be encoded for email
which mime headers identify hebrew email
subtitle: How the memo represents Hebrew text in MIME email.

tldr.problem: Email needs to identify the character set and transfer encoding used for Hebrew text so a recipient can interpret it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says to convert Hebrew text to ISO-8859-8 and use Quoted-Printable or Base64 with MIME headers that identify the character set and encoding.
tldr.outcome: It documents a method for transferring Hebrew text in email and describes visual directionality as the default.

today: RFC 1555 is Informational. It records a method for transferring Hebrew text through MIME email and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Representing Hebrew Text
sections.content:
The memo describes the character encoding used for transferring Hebrew in electronic mail. Hebrew text is first translated into ISO-8859-8 and then encoded using Quoted-Printable, which the RFC prefers, or Base64 as defined by MIME.

It includes a table comparing four common encodings for Hebrew letters and notes that ISO 8859-8 is also known as IBM Codepage 862.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender converts Hebrew text to ISO-8859-8, then encodes it for email transfer. MIME headers identify the encoding used.

sections.title: MIME Headers and Directionality
sections.content:
Mail containing Hebrew must include MIME-Version 1.0, a Content-type of text/plain with charset ISO-8859-8, and a Content-transfer-encoding of BASE64 or Quoted-Printable. The RFC describes the default directionality as visual: Hebrew is encoded and transmitted from left to right, even though it is entered from right to left.

The memo refers readers to RFC 1556 for other methods of controlling directionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers say that the message contains ISO-8859-8 text and identify how it was encoded. The memo's default sends the text in visual order from left to right.

sections.title: Mailing-List and Quoting Caveats
sections.content:
The RFC recommends keeping lines within 72 columns to allow email quoting. It warns that quoting Hebrew email may cause problems in MIME implementations.

It also explains that mailing-list software may remove MIME headers from delivered messages or archives, leaving user software without the information needed to interpret the encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Quoting and mailing-list processing can remove or disrupt information needed to read Hebrew messages. The RFC describes ways users could request full headers from a list.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 1555 is an informational memo. It describes an email encoding method and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo provides information about Hebrew email encoding. It does not define an Internet standard.
